 RJ Godfrey sues Arizona Board of Regents in latest push for eligibility
 by Brian Pedersen Nov 6, 2026, 1:31 AM UTC Facebook 
 Link 
 TUCSON, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 16: RJ Godfrey #0 of the Arizona Wildcats before the preseason game against the San Diego State Aztecs at McKale Center at ALKEME Arena on October 16, 2026 in Tucson, Arizona. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) Getty Images With his initial case in Georgia in limbo and the quest to join another in Texas denied, RJ Godfrey has opted to take legal action much closer to his current home as he seeks to gain eligibility for a fifth season. But rather than the NCAA, his named defendant is the Arizona Board of Regents.
 Godfrey and his attorneys on Thursday filed for suit in Pima County Superior Court against ABOR, the governing board that oversees the UA, seeking a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction and permanent injunction for eligibility. It his Godfrey’s third attempt to challenge the NCAA’s new “five for five” eligibility rule, which the NCAA has said does not apply to student-athletes who graduated high school in 2022.
 The judge assigned to the case is Jeffrey Bergin , the Presiding Judge of Pima County Superior Court. He is a graduate of the UA’s law school and also got his undergraduate degree there.
 The complaint cites a bylaw in the NCAA’s 2026-27 Division I manual regarding that does not make an exception for 2022 high school graduates. That’s been the approach most have taken to seek TROs and get eligible, but in most cases the NCAA has appealed and either won or—in the case of Godfrey’s initial case in Georgia—been granted a stay against an injunction.
 Where this new claim is different, though, is that Godfrey is seeking the TRO against ABOR and the university itself. The complaint seeks an order “requiring the University to perform its own contractual obligations” toward Godfrey and determine him eligible to play based on the plain text of the NCAA bylaw.
 In layman’s terms, the NCAA has said it’s really up to its member institutions to determine eligibility. Godfrey’s suit is asking ABOR and the UA to do that for him.
 The NCAA is not named as a party in the complaint but could still choose to weigh in.
 Godfrey, a 6-foot-8 forward who played three seasons at Clemson and one at Georgia, signed with Arizona in the summer but has not competed in any games including the overseas trip to Lithuania in August. He has remained with the program and practiced throughout, sitting on the bench for Monday’s season-opening loss to UCLA on Monday in Las Vegas.
 Arizona plays its home opener Thursday night against Cal Poly in ALKEME Arena at McKale Center. If Godfrey were to be granted a TRO the earliest he’d be able to play is Tuesday at home against NAU.
